title: The US retail calendar
summary: The American consumer year month by month, plus the retail fiscal-year conventions behind company results. Knowing the calendar lets you explain a quarterly swing in seconds instead of inventing an operational problem.

blocks.note: Easter moves between late March and late April, shifting sales between Q1 and Q2 and distorting year-on-year comparisons.

blocks.title: Size of the big moments (recent NRF / Adobe / IRS data)
items: Holiday season (Nov-Dec) 2025: retail sales passed ~$1 trillion for the first time, up ~4% (NRF / CNBC Retail Monitor).
Thanksgiving weekend 2025 (Thursday to Cyber Monday): a record ~203M shoppers, more online than in-store (NRF).
Cyber Monday 2025: ~$14B of US online spend, the biggest online day of the year (Adobe).
Prime Day 2025 (four days in July): ~$24B of US online spend across all retailers, not just Amazon (Adobe).
Halloween 2025: a record ~$13B, split roughly evenly across costumes, decorations and candy (NRF).
Valentine's Day 2026: a record ~$29B forecast, ~$200 per celebrant (NRF).
Tax season 2026: average refund ~$3,400 through mid-April, up ~11% on 2025 (IRS).

blocks.title: Tax-refund season is a real spending wave
blocks.body: Most US tax filers over-withhold during the year and get a lump-sum refund between February and April. For many lower- and middle-income households, it is the biggest cheque of the year. Retailers of cars, furniture, electronics and apparel see a visible bump, and dollar stores and discounters feel it when refunds arrive late or shrink. Refunds that include the Earned Income Tax Credit start flowing from late February.

blocks.title: Retail fiscal years and the 4-5-4 calendar
blocks.body: Most US retailers end their fiscal year around January 31 (Walmart, Target, Kroger, Dollar General), so the full holiday season and January returns land in one year. Watch naming: Walmart's 'fiscal 2026' ended January 2026. Costco's year ends around August 31; Amazon uses the calendar year. Retailers report in 4-5-4 months (weeks per month in each quarter) so every period has the same number of weekends.

blocks.title: 4-5-4 essentials
items: Each quarter is 13 weeks split 4-5-4; the year is 52 weeks and starts in early February (NRF calendar).
A 53rd week is added roughly every five to six years (most recently 2023), inflating that year's sales.
Comparisons are week-aligned: 'comparable sales' compares the same retail weeks, not calendar dates.
Thanksgiving's date (Nov 22-28) changes how many shopping days fall between it and Christmas.

blocks.title: Q4 is not the same quarter everywhere
blocks.body: For a January-year-end retailer, Q4 is November to January and holds the holiday peak. For Costco, Q4 is June to August; for Amazon it is October to December. Before comparing two companies' 'Q4,' map each to actual months, and check for a 53rd week or an Easter shift.

blocks.title: Ask about timing before diagnosing
blocks.body: When a case shows a sales drop or spike, ask: which months, which fiscal calendar, and how does it compare with the same period last year? Then check holidays (Easter, Thanksgiving date), weather, tax refunds and promotional events. Saying 'Q1 is seasonally weak after holiday pull-forward' early shows commercial instinct.

in_a_case: A grocer's Q1 dip: post-holiday hangover plus January budget resets; check the calendar before blaming operations.
A toy or electronics retailer: a large share of annual sales sits in Nov-Dec, so inventory planning and holiday returns dominate the economics.
A discounter's weak February: late or smaller tax refunds hit lower-income shoppers' spending.
Comparing two retailers' 'Q4': align fiscal calendars and adjust for any 53rd week before drawing conclusions.
A promotion-timing question: anchor around tentpoles (Prime Day in July, Black Friday, back-to-school) when competitors also discount.
